wave.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
wave.body: Three boats plunge through a storm-tossed sea while a cresting wave curls overhead and Mount Fuji sits small and still on the horizon. The first print in Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, and the work that carried Prussian blue into Japanese printmaking.

turner.title: Rain, Steam and Speed
turner.maker: J. M. W. Turner · 1844 · The National Gallery
turner.body: A steam train tears across a viaduct through a haze of rain and light — Turner dissolving the machine age into pure atmosphere. Look closely and a hare runs ahead of the engine on the tracks, outpacing it for now.

nebula.title: The Pillars of Creation
nebula.maker: Eagle Nebula · NASA / ESA · Public domain
nebula.body: Columns of cold hydrogen and dust light-years tall, lit and eroded at once by the young stars just outside the frame. Stars are forming inside them even as the pillars themselves are being worn away.

sky.title: Why the sky is blue
sky.lede: The sky isn't coloured — it's scattered. Shorter blue wavelengths bounce off air molecules far more than red ones.
sky.body: This is Rayleigh scattering: the intensity of scattered light climbs steeply as wavelength shrinks, so blue and violet dominate the daytime sky. At sunset the light travels a far longer path through the atmosphere — the blue is scattered away entirely before it reaches you.

engine.title: The internal-combustion engine
engine.lede: For over a century a controlled explosion, a few thousand times a minute, has moved most of the world.
engine.body: Fuel and air are drawn into a cylinder, compressed, then ignited. The expanding gas drives a piston; the piston turns a crank; the crank turns a wheel. Every refinement since is a variation on that single, insistent beat.

wayfinding.title: Polynesian wayfinding
wayfinding.lede: Navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific reading only the swell, the stars and the colour of the water.
wayfinding.body: A wayfinder memorised a 'star compass' — the points on the horizon where key stars rise and set — and held course by them through the night. By day they read the interference of ocean swells against unseen islands.
